title.en: The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages · three lessons

description.en: Lesson 1.1 The skin as a steroidogenic, endocrine organ · Lesson 1.2 Receptor maps and what they prove · Lesson 1.3 Senescence, the SASP and the ageing dermis.

unit.tutorContext: Module 1 teaches cutaneous neuro-immuno-endocrine physiology with every finding labelled by evidence type (mechanism, human evidence, regulatory status, open question). The skin is described as four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) that signal locally, via sensory nerves and via the circulation (mechanism reviews, D). Skin cells express CYP11A1, 11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase and aromatase and make cortisol, DHT and estradiol locally (cell/tissue work, D); human scalp follicles run an HPA-like loop with cortisol secretion and CRH feedback ex vivo (Ito 2005) and a GH/IGF-1 loop ex vivo (Horesh 2023); keratinocyte glucocorticoids restrain skin inflammation in mice (Phan 2021); the thyroid-like loop is mostly mouse data. Three directions: local loop; body to skin (Cushing striae, hypothyroid skin); skin to body (vitamin D3 released into the circulation, established human physiology; a skin contribution to circulating sex steroids per reviews). Refer systemic patterns promptly (violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapid virilisation), per the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide. The Hormone Cell Atlas (Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026) read RNA of 379 hormone/receptor genes in ~14 million cells and nuclei from 47 tissues incl. skin; its authors call the predictions putative and hypothesis-generating: RNA is not protein, secretion or clinical effect. The guide's pearl that serum 25(OH)D falls with sunscreen use is not borne out by field trials of daily moderate-SPF sunscreen (Neale 2019, C; high SPF untested); never advise dropping sun protection. Senescence: p16-positive cells rise with age in human epidermis and dermis (C) and track with wrinkles and perceived age (Waaijer 2016, n=178, association, C); the SASP was defined in cultured cells (D); an MMP-1 collagen-fragmentation loop is shown in aged human dermis plus culture (D), with senescent cells a plausible, unproven driver; clearing senescent cells extends healthy lifespan in mice (D); human senotherapy data are small biomarker pilots (Hickson 2019 open-label n=9, D; Chung 2019 topical rapamycin exploratory RCT, C); no randomized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes (checked Sept 2026); the guide confines senolytics to trials. Levers with human trials: daily sunscreen (Hughes 2013, n=903, B), topical tretinoin for photoageing (GRADE A), retinol in very old skin (Kafi 2007, C). Never give doses, concentrations, regimens or sourcing; adapt 'what you do next' to the learner's role (prescriber, clinical staff, advisor) without changing evidence. No CME credit is currently offered.

lead.en: Hormones and Peptides for Skin · Module 01

title.en: The skin makes its own hormones.

body.en: This course starts with physiology, because every later question about a hormone or peptide for skin rests on it. Skin senses hormones from the blood, makes several of its own, and ages in ways that change both. In three lessons you will separate what happens locally in the skin from what the rest of the body sends in, and label each finding by the kind of evidence behind it.

points.en: 1.1 The skin as a steroidogenic, endocrine organ
1.2 Receptor maps: what a cell atlas can and cannot show
1.3 Senescence, the SASP and the ageing dermis

body.en: Recent reviews describe the skin as a neuro-immuno-endocrine organ built from four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal (hair follicles and glands). Each holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response. They signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the blood. Most of this picture comes from cell, tissue and animal studies.

points.en: Four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal
Three routes: neighbour to neighbour, nerve, bloodstream
Mechanism register: cell, tissue and animal work

blocks.sourceNote: Slominski 2025 · Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Zouboulis 2004 · Roosterman 2006 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5–6

body.en: Epidermis, dermis, subcutis and the adnexa each hold cells that make hormones and cells that react to them, from keratinocytes and fibroblasts to fat cells and mast cells.
Signals pass between neighbouring cells, along sensory nerves, and into the blood, where they can reach distant organs.
The framework is drawn from cell, tissue and animal work. It explains how skin behaves; each finding in this module is labelled by the evidence behind it.

audioScript.en: Think of the skin as a sensing organ with its own hormone supply. Researchers who study it describe four units, epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal, the last meaning hair follicles and glands. Each unit holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response, such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts, sebocytes, fat cells and mast cells. Signals move three ways. Neighbouring cells talk directly, sensory nerves carry messages in and out, and some products enter the blood and reach distant organs. Keep one distinction in view for the whole module. A signal that is made and used inside the skin is a local loop. A hormone that arrives from the blood, or leaves the skin for the rest of the body, is systemic signalling. Much of what follows is mechanism, drawn from cell, tissue and animal studies, and each finding will be labelled that way.

title.en: A steroid factory with local axes.

body.en: Skin cells carry the enzymes to build steroids from cholesterol or to activate precursors arriving in the blood, and they run shortened copies of the body's central hormone axes. Each row names the evidence it rests on, because most of it comes from cells, tissue kept alive outside the body, or mice.

blocks.sourceNote: Slominski 2013 · Ito 2005 · Phan 2021 · Mancino 2021 · Horesh 2023 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6

label.en: Steroid synthesis

value.en: Cholesterol to cortisol, androgens and estrogens

note.en: CYP11A1 starts the chain; 11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase and aromatase activate precursors from the blood. Cell and tissue studies.

label.en: HPA-like loop

note.en: Human scalp follicles kept alive in culture. Ex vivo, human tissue.

label.en: Keratinocyte glucocorticoids

note.en: Genetic deletion in mouse keratinocytes. Animal evidence.

label.en: Thyroid-like loop

note.en: Keratinocyte growth and the hair cycle. Mostly mouse models.

label.en: Somatotropic loop
Melanocortins

note.en: Pigment, barrier and local immune restraint. Module 05 returns to this.

callout.en: A local axis explains biology. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide calls it foundation, not a dosing rationale.

body.en: Hormone signals in skin run in three directions. Some are made and used in the same patch of skin. Some arrive from the blood. A few leave the skin and act on the rest of the body. Knowing which one you are looking at decides whether the answer lies in the skin or in a systemic assessment.

value.en: Made and used in the skin

prompt.en: One finding at a time: which way does the signal run?

label.en: Local loop
Body to skin
Skin to body
Keratinocytes make cortisol that restrains immune cells in the same patch of skin

why.en: Local loop. Made and used where it is produced; the functional proof comes from mice that cannot make it in keratinocytes and develop skin inflammation.

label.en: UVB turns 7-dehydrocholesterol into vitamin D3, which the blood carries to the liver

why.en: Skin to body. Vitamin D3 made in the skin is released into the circulation and activated elsewhere. Established human physiology.

label.en: Violaceous striae, thin skin and easy bruising in Cushing syndrome

why.en: Body to skin. Systemic cortisol excess acting on the dermis. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide lists suspected Cushing syndrome as a reason to refer promptly.

label.en: Scalp hair follicles kept alive in culture secrete cortisol, then switch off their own CRH

why.en: Local loop, with its own feedback, running with no blood supply or nerves attached. Human tissue, ex vivo.

label.en: Skin converts circulating precursors into androgens and estrogens that add to the body's supply

why.en: Skin to body. Reviews describe a skin contribution to circulating sex steroids, more so in older people; the evidence is mainly biochemical.

label.en: Dry, coarse skin and myxoedema in hypothyroidism

why.en: Body to skin. Circulating thyroid hormone sets epidermal turnover and dermal matrix; the skin signs track the systemic deficit.

label.en: Scalp follicles convert testosterone to DHT, which shrinks susceptible follicles

why.en: Local loop. 5α-reductase in the pilosebaceous unit makes DHT where it acts; the guide names it the substrate of acne, androgenetic alopecia and hirsutism.

done.en: Seven placed. Three local loops, two signals the skin sends out, and two it receives.

title.en: Read the skin before the serum.

body.en: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen. Sudden thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess; coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism; new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance. It lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, and rapidly progressive virilisation, among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. Local skin biology explains how skin behaves; it does not justify prescribing a hormone.

points.en: A skin sign can be the first sign of a systemic disorder
Some patterns need prompt endocrine referral
Local loops explain biology; they do not justify treatment

blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5 clinical pearl and referral list · Safer 2011

body.en: Thinning and bruising, coarse dry skin, new acanthosis nigricans: each points to a systemic axis before it points to a serum.
The guide lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapid virilisation and signs of an endocrine tumour as reasons to refer promptly.
Local loops explain how skin behaves day to day. The guide calls them foundation, never a reason to dose anyone with a hormone.

audioScript.en: Picture the consultation where a patient asks about thinning, bruising skin. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide asks you to read that skin as a window on the whole endocrine system before reaching for a serum. Sudden thinning with easy bruising suggests cortisol excess. Coarse, dry, cool skin suggests an underactive thyroid. New acanthosis nigricans points to insulin resistance. The guide lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapidly progressive virilisation, and signs of an endocrine tumour as reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. The local loops from the last two moments explain how skin behaves day to day. They are foundation biology, and the guide is explicit that they are no rationale for dosing anyone with a hormone. Whatever your role, a systemic pattern in the skin gets a systemic answer.

prescriber.en: When a skin pattern suggests a systemic disorder, assess or refer before any cosmetic plan, and record that you considered it. Local skin biology is no basis for prescribing a hormone for appearance.

clinical-staff.en: If you see new striae, rapid bruising, sudden hair change or signs of virilisation, record them and raise them with the prescriber before the next treatment.

advisor.en: If a client's skin change comes with new systemic symptoms, suggest they see a prescriber before trying another product. A serum cannot answer a systemic question.

body.en: One question to close lesson 1.1.

prompt.en: Fictional case. A 52-year-old has new thin, easily bruised skin on her forearms, new violaceous striae and newly raised blood pressure. She has read that skin makes its own cortisol and asks whether a cream could calm it. Which reading is right?

text.en: Her skin's own cortisol explains the picture, so the answer is local.

why.en: Local skin cortisol tunes immune activity where it is made. It does not explain new striae together with new hypertension.

text.en: The combination is a systemic pattern; the guide lists it as a reason for prompt endocrine referral before any skin treatment.

why.en: Correct. Striae, bruising and new hypertension together point to possible systemic cortisol excess: a body-to-skin signal.

text.en: Local and systemic cortisol are interchangeable, so either explanation fits.

why.en: Local synthesis acts within the skin and runs its own feedback; a systemic syndrome needs a systemic assessment.

feedback.en: Decide which direction the signal runs before you decide what to treat.

title.en: A map of fourteen million cells.

body.en: The Hormone Cell Atlas, published in Science in 2026, read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them. From that RNA it predicted which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond to one. It is a map of predicted capacity; it did not measure hormone release.

points.en: RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes
About 14 million cells and nuclei, 47 tissues
Output: predicted producers and receivers

blocks.sourceNote: Fei & Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · hormonecellatlas.org.uk · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

body.en: RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes, cell by cell, across 47 human tissues including skin.
Which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond, including unexpected sites outside the classic glands.
Whether a cell actually makes and releases the hormone, and whether that hormone does anything there.

audioScript.en: Fourteen million cells is the scale of the Hormone Cell Atlas, a Cambridge-led study published in Science in 2026. The team read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in single cells and nuclei from forty-seven human tissues, skin included. From those readings they scored each cell type for its predicted capacity to make or to receive a hormone, and they flagged unexpected sites, such as RNA for the gut hormone secretin in a type of immune cell. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide uses the atlas to argue that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed signalling networks. The word plausibly matters. Everything in the atlas starts from RNA, and RNA tells you what a cell could make. Whether the cell actually makes and releases the hormone is the question the rest of this lesson answers.

title.en: Prediction, in the authors' own words.

body.en: The atlas's own portal describes its scores as 'putative and hypothesis-generating'. A few predictions were tested in cells in the paper itself; the rest are left for users to validate. Across biology, the amount of RNA for a gene is often a poor guide to how much protein a cell makes, and protein is still a step short of secretion.

blocks.sourceNote: Fei & Huang-Doran, Science 2026 · hormonecellatlas.org.uk About/FAQ, read 24 Sep 2026 · Liu 2016

label.en: hormone and receptor genes read as RNA, cell by cell

detail.en: Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · about 14 million cells and nuclei · 47 human tissues

means.en: The atlas shows which skin cells carry the RNA to make or sense a hormone. That is a well-founded hypothesis about where to look.

doesNot.en: It does not show that a skin cell secretes a hormone, how much, or that the hormone acts there. A receptor gene on the map is not evidence that a product aimed at it works.

body.en: Findings about skin as an endocrine organ sit on different rungs of the same ladder. Before you see the answers, decide how far up each one reaches.

blocks.sourceNote: Fei 2026 · atlas portal · Ito 2005 · Phan 2021 · Horesh 2023 · Holick 1980 · Bikle 2014

label.en: Transcript

note.en: Single-cell atlases; a prediction to confirm

label.en: Function in tissue or animals

note.en: Human tissue kept alive in culture, or animal models

label.en: Human, in vivo

note.en: Measured in people, in the body

callout.en: Each rung needs the one below it, and advice to a patient needs the top one.

prompt.en: Tap the highest rung each finding reaches.

Function in tissue or animals
Human, in vivo
A skin cell type scores high as a hormone producer in a single-cell RNA atlas

why.en: Transcript. The score comes from RNA; the atlas's authors call such predictions putative until validated.

label.en: Scalp hair follicles kept alive in culture secrete cortisol and switch off their own CRH

why.en: Function in human tissue. The loop works ex vivo; whether it shapes hair growth in a living scalp is a further step.

label.en: A brochure says skin 'has receptors for' a hormone, citing an RNA atlas

why.en: Transcript. A receptor gene on a map is where the question starts, and where this brochure stops.

label.en: Mice unable to make glucocorticoids in keratinocytes develop skin inflammation

why.en: Function in animals. Strong evidence that local glucocorticoids matter in mouse skin; in people there is only an association with inflammatory skin disease.

why.en: Human, in vivo. Cutaneous vitamin D3 synthesis and its release into the circulation were shown in human skin and are established physiology.

title.en: A map to confirm, then a trial.

body.en: Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts, so the skin's response need not mirror the dose. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts. The same caution applies to physiology you think you know: the guide says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, yet field trials of daily sunscreen did not lower it.

points.en: A receptor on the map is a hypothesis
Local enzymes change potency in skin
Daily-sunscreen field trials did not lower vitamin D

blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6–7 pearls · Neale 2019 · Fei 2026 · Bikle 2014

body.en: Receptors explain how a topical could act. Whether it does is a question for a human trial.
Steroid-metabolising enzymes in skin change potency, so the response in skin can differ from what the dose predicts.
Artificial-UV experiments show sunscreen blocks vitamin D synthesis; field trials of daily use did not lower blood levels. High-protection products have not been trialled.

audioScript.en: Two habits follow from the atlas. The first concerns product claims. Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts once it arrives, so the response in skin can differ from what the dose predicts. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts, and the answer still needs a trial. The second habit concerns the physiology you think you know. The guide's testing pearl says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, which the biology predicts. An independent review found that in real-life field trials, daily sunscreen did not lower blood levels, although the sunscreens tested were moderate and today's high-protection products have never been trialled. Keep recommending sun protection, and treat vitamin D as its own question.

prescriber.en: When a product or protocol is justified by 'skin has receptors for it', ask for the human trial before you prescribe. Assess vitamin D on clinical grounds, and do not advise patients to drop sun protection.

clinical-staff.en: If a patient says they stopped sunscreen to raise their vitamin D, note it and pass it to the prescriber; the trials do not support stopping.

advisor.en: Describe receptor-based product claims as hypotheses unless a human trial backs them, keep sun-protection advice unchanged, and send vitamin D questions to a prescriber.

body.en: One question to close lesson 1.2.

prompt.en: A brochure for a hormone-containing serum cites a single-cell atlas showing that dermal fibroblasts carry the RNA for that hormone's receptor. What does that finding establish?

text.en: That the serum reaches those fibroblasts and improves the skin.

why.en: That needs penetration data and a clinical trial; an RNA map provides neither.

text.en: That skin secretes the hormone and needs it replaced when levels fall.

why.en: The finding concerns a receptor, and RNA says nothing about secretion or deficiency.

text.en: That fibroblasts may respond to the hormone: a hypothesis to confirm at the protein, function and clinical level.

why.en: Correct. The atlas's authors call such predictions putative and hypothesis-generating.

feedback.en: A receptor on the map is where the question starts.

title.en: Cells that stop dividing and keep talking.

body.en: A senescent cell has stopped dividing for good but stays metabolically active, releasing cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors: the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, or SASP. The SASP was characterised in cultured cells. In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a become more common with age in both epidermis and dermis.

points.en: Senescent: permanent arrest, still secreting
SASP (IL-6, IL-8, MMPs, growth factors): defined in culture
Human skin: p16-positive cells rise with age

blocks.sourceNote: Coppé 2008 · Ressler 2006 · Ho & Dreesen 2021 · Wang & Dreesen 2018 · Haykal 2026 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

body.en: A damaged cell stops dividing for good, which guards against cancer and helps wound repair.
It stays active and releases inflammatory cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors, first catalogued in cultured human cells.

title.en: What we see in human skin

body.en: Older skin holds more cells carrying the marker p16 in epidermis and dermis. No single marker is definitive.

audioScript.en: Senescence begins as a safety mechanism. A cell that has taken enough damage stops dividing for good, which helps guard against cancer and is useful during wound repair. The problem is what the cell does next. It stays alive and metabolically busy and releases a mixture of inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin six and eight, enzymes that break down matrix, and growth factors. This secretory profile, the SASP, was characterised in human cells grown in the laboratory after DNA damage. In living human skin, the evidence is observational. Skin samples from older people contain more cells carrying the senescence marker p16, in both the epidermis and the dermis, and fibroblasts, keratinocytes and melanocytes can all become senescent. Researchers also caution that no single marker identifies a senescent cell with certainty, so counts depend on the marker chosen.

body.en: In a Dutch cohort, people with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and looked older, after allowing for their actual age. The epidermal p16-positive cells were mostly melanocytes. The study was publicly funded; one co-author worked for Unilever.

label.en: younger-looking: fewest versus most p16-positive epidermal cells, at the same chronological age

detail.en: Waaijer et al., 2016 — 178 adults aged 45–81, Leiden Longevity Study, sun-protected arm biopsies

means.en: Senescent-cell burden in human skin tracks visible ageing, even in skin that sees little sun.

doesNot.en: It does not show that senescent cells cause wrinkles, or that removing them would reverse any. One observational cohort shows an association.

body.en: Senescence research mixes human tissue, mice and cultured cells. For the ageing dermis the four answers point in different directions, which is why they belong in separate sentences.

blocks.sourceNote: Shuster 1975 · Varani 2006 · Fisher 2009 · Waaijer 2016 · Baker 2016 · Xu 2018 · Hickson 2019 · Chung 2019

label.en: Mechanism

note.en: Skin collagen falls with age. Aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1 and fragmented collagen; in culture, fragmentation raises MMP-1 further. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible, not shown.

label.en: Human evidence

note.en: p16-positive cells rise with age and track with wrinkles and perceived age

label.en: Animal evidence

note.en: Clearing p16-positive cells, or giving senolytic drugs, extends healthy lifespan in mice. Skin was checked only for safety, and clearing these cells during healing slowed wound closure.

label.en: Open question

note.en: Small pilots measuring tissue markers. One exploratory randomized trial of topical rapamycin (36 enrolled, 19 dropped out) lowered skin p16, and clinical change was only described. No adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found (September 2026).

callout.en: A mouse lifespan result is not a skin treatment.

title.en: The levers with trials behind them.

body.en: Two ways of protecting or rebuilding the dermal matrix have randomized human trials. In a community trial of 903 adults, daily sunscreen for four and a half years slowed photoageing compared with discretionary use (GRADE B). Topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, GRADE A. Retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small trial (C), and within a week it raised collagen synthesis and lowered MMPs in biopsies of aged human skin.

points.en: Daily sunscreen: one large RCT (B)
Topical retinoids for photoageing: GRADE A
Senolytics for skin: no clinical-outcome trials yet

blocks.sourceNote: Hughes 2013 · Sitohang 2022 · Kafi 2007 · Varani 2000 · Fisher 2002 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5

body.en: A publicly funded Australian trial of 903 adults: daily sunscreen meant about a quarter less skin ageing over four and a half years.
Consistent randomized trials for tretinoin in photoaged skin; the guide's GRADE A. Retinol has smaller trials, including one in very old skin.
Biomarker pilots only, so far. They sit below the levers that already have outcome data.

audioScript.en: Set the senescence story beside the interventions that have been tested in people. In Nambour, Australia, a publicly funded trial randomised 903 adults to daily or discretionary sunscreen, and over four and a half years skin ageing was about a quarter lower with daily use. Topical tretinoin has a run of randomised trials in photoaged skin that agree with one another, and the Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, grade A. Retinol has smaller trials, including one in residents in their late eighties whose fine wrinkling improved and whose biopsies showed more procollagen. Both levers protect or rebuild the dermal matrix that ultraviolet light and, it is thought, the SASP erode, and both have human outcome data. Senolytics for skin have no such data yet. Keep that order in mind when a patient asks what actually works.

body.en: A 58-year-old patient has read that senolytic supplements 'clear zombie cells' and reverse skin ageing, and asks whether to start one she found online. She does not use sunscreen daily. The case is fictional and built from the lesson's evidence; decide your first move.

points.en: Senescent cells in human skin: real, and linked with visible ageing
Clearing them: mouse evidence and small human biomarker pilots
Sunscreen and retinoids: randomized human trials

Senescent cells track with visible ageing in human skin; clearing them helps in mice; human data are small biomarker pilots.
Daily sunscreen and topical retinoids have randomized trials with visible skin outcomes.

setup.en: A 58-year-old patient has read that senolytic supplements 'clear zombie cells' and reverse skin ageing, and asks whether to start one she found online. She does not use sunscreen daily.

notice.en: Senescent cells do accumulate in human skin and track with wrinkles and perceived age
The evidence that clearing them helps comes from mice; human studies are small pilots measuring tissue markers
Daily sunscreen and topical retinoids have randomized trials with visible skin outcomes

label.en: Support a trial of the supplement: senescent cells clearly age skin, so clearing them should help.

why.en: The human evidence is an association and the clearing evidence is in mice. No trial has tested senolytics on skin-ageing outcomes.

label.en: Explain what is known in people and what only in mice, point her to the measures with trials (daily sunscreen, and a topical retinoid discussed with a prescriber), and mention that senolytics are being studied in trials.

why.en: Right. It keeps the registers apart and moves her toward the levers with human outcome data. The guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.

label.en: Tell her senescence is a mouse phenomenon with no relevance to human skin.

why.en: Senescent cells are measurable in human skin and track with wrinkles and perceived age. The biology is real; the treatment evidence is what is missing.

followUp.en: Then record what she was considering and what you advised, including any product she has already bought.

audioScript.en: Consider a fifty-eight-year-old patient, fictional and built from this lesson's evidence. She has read that senolytic supplements clear so-called zombie cells and reverse skin ageing, and she asks whether to start one she found online. She does not wear sunscreen every day. Three facts frame the conversation. Senescent cells really do accumulate in human skin, and their number tracks with wrinkles and with how old a person looks. The evidence that clearing them helps comes from mice, and the human studies so far are small pilots measuring markers in tissue. Daily sunscreen and topical retinoids, by contrast, have randomised trials with visible skin outcomes. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises keeping senolytics within clinical trials. Decide what you say first.

prescriber.en: You weigh a prescription retinoid against her skin and history, document the discussion, and explain that senolytics are still at the pilot-study stage and belong in trials.

clinical-staff.en: You record what she plans to buy and anything she already takes, share the evidence summary, and pass the retinoid question to the prescriber.

advisor.en: You explain the difference between mouse and human evidence, reinforce daily sunscreen, and suggest a prescriber for a retinoid or if she wants to explore a trial.

prompt.en: Which statement about senescence and skin ageing matches the evidence?

text.en: Randomized trials show that senolytics reverse human skin ageing.

why.en: No randomized trial of a senolytic with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found. Human data are small pilots measuring tissue markers.

text.en: Senescence has been seen only in mice and cultured cells.

why.en: p16-positive cells are measurable in human skin and become more common with age.

text.en: In human skin, senescent cells increase with age and track with wrinkles; the evidence that clearing them improves ageing comes from mice.

why.en: Correct. Human association, mouse causation: two registers, kept apart.

feedback.en: Name the species before you weigh the finding.

interaction.source: authored:2026-09-24 from Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology ch. 5–7 pearls and m1 tool items

prompt.en: Closing Module 1 (fictional case). A 41-year-old with a low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D says she will stop sunscreen because 'skin makes vitamin D'. Which reply keeps the physiology and the evidence straight?

text.en: Vitamin D made in skin stays in the skin, so sunscreen cannot affect her blood level.

why.en: Skin-made vitamin D3 enters the circulation: the skin is acting as an endocrine gland for the whole body.

text.en: Skin synthesis does feed her blood level, but field trials of daily sunscreen did not lower 25-hydroxyvitamin D; keep sun protection and treat the low level as its own clinical question.

why.en: Correct. The signal runs skin to body, and the human trials, not the mechanism alone, set the advice.

text.en: The guide says sunscreen lowers vitamin D, so stopping it is reasonable.

why.en: Real-life trials did not show a fall, and the guide itself says this biology never licenses unprotected sun exposure.

feedback.en: Name the direction of the signal, then let the human evidence set the advice.

prompt.en: A single-cell RNA atlas predicts that a skin cell type can make a hormone. What would move that finding toward proof of secretion?

text.en: Showing the hormone protein and its release by those cells, then its effect in tissue or in people.

why.en: Correct. RNA is the first rung; protein, release and function are the next.

text.en: Finding the same RNA in a second atlas.

why.en: Replicating the RNA confirms the transcript, which is still a prediction about secretion.

text.en: Finding the hormone's receptor RNA in neighbouring cells.

why.en: That predicts a possible receiver; it does not show the hormone is made or released.

rationale.en: Transcriptomic maps predict capacity; secretion and function need protein-level and functional evidence, and clinical use needs human trials.

prompt.en: Which finding is a local cutaneous feedback loop rather than systemic endocrine signalling?

text.en: Skin-made vitamin D3 carried by the blood to the liver.

why.en: That is the skin supplying a whole-body hormone system: skin to body.

text.en: Human scalp follicles in culture secrete cortisol and then reduce their own CRH.

why.en: Correct. Made, sensed and fed back within the follicle, with no systemic connection.

text.en: Thin skin and striae in Cushing syndrome.

why.en: Circulating cortisol excess acting on the skin: body to skin.

rationale.en: A local loop is made and used within the skin; systemic signals travel through the blood, in either direction.

answer.en: The Hormone Cell Atlas (Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026) read RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues and predicted which cell types could make or respond to hormones. Its own authors call these predictions putative and hypothesis-generating: RNA shows capacity, not secretion or effect. Treat any 'skin has receptors for it' product claim as a hypothesis until protein, function and a human trial back it. A few skin outputs are established in people, such as vitamin D3 formed under UVB and released into the blood.

Senescent cells accumulate in human epidermis and dermis with age, and in one cohort their number tracked with wrinkles and perceived age: an association. Their secretions (the SASP: IL-6, IL-8, matrix-degrading enzymes) were defined in cultured cells. Evidence that clearing senescent cells improves ageing comes from mice; human data are small open-label or exploratory pilots measuring tissue markers. The one randomized study in skin (topical rapamycin, a senomorphic, 2019) was small and exploratory: it lowered p16, and clinical change was only described. No adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found (September 2026). In mice, clearing senescent cells during healing slowed wound closure. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises confining senolytics to clinical trials. This course gives no doses or product advice; daily sunscreen and topical retinoids are the levers with human trials, and a prescriber decides on any treatment.

reviewNotes.change: The automated source check, which matches every cited sentence against the source's own text, contradicted two statements. Both are corrected. (1) Baker 2016 did measure skin: thickness, fibrosis and wound closure as safety checks, and clearance during healing slowed wound closure, so the course no longer says skin was not an endpoint. (2) Chung 2019 topical rapamycin was an exploratory randomized trial with clinical appearance described qualitatively. The course now says no adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found, and keeps 'no randomized senolytic trial' where the statement is about senolytics.
Source-check alignment: vitamin D3 'to the liver' (the cited source names the liver step); atlas tutor answer no longer adds 'including skin' beyond the abstract.
